title: Transient heat and the θ-method
summary: March a driven bar through time with the θ-method, then run the same problem again with backward Euler and see what the choice of θ and Δt actually costs you.

steps.title: Start a Model
steps.explain: This is NAFEMS benchmark T3: a bar driven by a temperature that swings as a sine, held at zero at the far end. It has a published answer, which is what makes it worth building rather than inventing your own transient.

steps.title: Units, including time
steps.explain: `model.setUnits` takes a `time` entry. Every `dt`, `tEnd` and history time is read and printed in it.

steps.title: Add the bar
steps.explain: 100 mm long and a thin 5 × 5 mm section — the published benchmark is one-dimensional, and a thin bar with no side boundary conditions is the 3D way to say that. Faces with no Command on them are insulated, so no heat escapes sideways.

steps.title: A material with heat capacity
steps.explain: Time enters through `rho` and `cp`. The combination that matters is the thermal diffusivity `α = k/(ρ·cp)`, in m²/s: it sets how fast a disturbance spreads, and every transient timescale in the problem is `L²/α`. Here that is about 90 s, which is why a 32 s run is interesting and a 0.1 s run would show nothing.

steps.title: Assign it
steps.explain: One Material on the one Body.

steps.title: Mesh it: twenty elements along
steps.explain: Space and time have to be resolved together. A rule of thumb for the θ-method is that `α·Δt` should be comparable to the square of the element size — much smaller and the fine elements are wasted, much larger and a sharp front is smeared over an element. Twenty elements at Δt = 0.5 s is in the right region for this bar.

steps.title: The driven face
steps.explain: `constraint.temperature` with a value of "100 K" — a *difference*, not an absolute temperature, because this Step runs in kelvin above the initial state. In a transient Step the prescribed value is multiplied by the Step's `amplitude`, so this face follows `100·g(t)`.

steps.title: The held face
steps.explain: The other end stays at zero for the whole run. `0 K` times any amplitude is still zero.

steps.title: The transient Step: Crank–Nicolson
steps.explain: `procedure: "heat-transient"` needs `dt`, `tEnd` and an `initial` temperature; `theta` picks the integrator and `amplitude` is the time function. `theta: 0.5` is Crank–Nicolson. `outputEvery: 16` keeps every sixteenth step in the history rather than all 64, which is what a plot wants. The `amplitude` is data, never a formula you type: a sine or a table, so the Journal replays identically anywhere.

steps.title: Solve it and read the history
steps.explain: The Result now has a `history`: one entry per kept step, with its time and the extremes of the field. Probe 20 mm inside the driven face (x = 80 mm) at the end of the run — about 36.8 K, against the published 36.60. Under 1 % on a benchmark whose reference is quoted to three figures.

steps.title: Now the same run with backward Euler
steps.explain: Identical Step, identical time step, `theta: 1.0`. Nothing else changes, so any difference in the answer is the integrator and nothing else.

steps.title: Compare
steps.explain: Solve it and probe the same point. Backward Euler lands a little further from the reference: it is first-order accurate, so halving Δt halves its error, while Crank–Nicolson is second-order and halving Δt quarters its error. Both are unconditionally stable — neither will ever blow up, however big Δt is — which is the whole reason to use an implicit method for heat.

steps.title: What θ actually is
steps.explain: One parameter, three well-known schemes, and one trade-off between accuracy and well-behavedness.
steps.theory:
Transient conduction is $\rho c_p \dot T = \nabla\cdot(k\,\nabla T) + \dot q$. Discretised in space it becomes
$$\mathbf{C}\,\dot{\mathbf{T}} + \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{f}(t)$$
with $\mathbf{C}$ the capacity matrix (it holds $\rho c_p$) and $\mathbf{K}$ the conductivity matrix. The $\theta$-method evaluates the right-hand side at a point $\theta$ of the way through the step:
$$\left(\mathbf{C} + \theta\,\Delta t\,\mathbf{K}\right)\mathbf{T}^{n+1} = \left(\mathbf{C} - (1-\theta)\,\Delta t\,\mathbf{K}\right)\mathbf{T}^{n} + \Delta t\left(\theta\,\mathbf{f}^{n+1} + (1-\theta)\,\mathbf{f}^{n}\right)$$

| $\theta$ | scheme | order | stability |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0$ | forward Euler | 1 | conditional: $\Delta t \le \dfrac{2}{\lambda_{max}}$, brutally small |
| $0.5$ | Crank–Nicolson | 2 | unconditional, but not damped |
| $2/3$ | Galerkin | 2 | unconditional, mildly damped |
| $1$ | backward Euler | 1 | unconditional, strongly damped |

**Crank–Nicolson is the accurate one, and it is the one that rings.** At $\theta = 0.5$ the amplification factor of the stiffest mode tends to $-1$ as $\Delta t$ grows: an error in that mode does not decay, it flips sign every step. Apply a step change in temperature with a large $\Delta t$ and the first few steps oscillate about the answer instead of approaching it. It is stable — the oscillation does not grow — but it is visible and it is wrong.

**Backward Euler is the safe one.** Its stiff modes are annihilated in one step, so a step change is handled without a wobble; the price is first-order accuracy, so you pay for the smoothness in time steps.

The practical rule: $\theta = 0.5$ for a smooth drive like this sine, $\theta = 1$ (or $2/3$) for the first few steps after a shock, and always confirm by halving $\Delta t$ and seeing the answer stop moving. A time step study is the same discipline as a mesh study, and just as non-optional.
